06 — Overview ​

How sessions work, and what belongs in one. Read this before you write code.

A session is a log, not a snapshot ​

There are two ways to persist a conversation. You can save the current state, or you can save every change that produced it.

Snapshots are smaller and easier to read. Logs win on two properties that matter here:

PropertySnapshotAppend-only log
A crash mid-writethe file is half-written and uselessthe last line is lost, the rest is fine
Two readersmust agree on a lockboth read the same prefix
History of how you got herelostkept

So the format is one JSON object per line:

{"type":"header","version":1,"created":"2026-10-27T10:00:00Z"}
{"type":"message","message":{"role":"user","content":"which branch?"}}
{"type":"message","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"release"}}

JSONL also means tail -f work.jsonl is a debugging tool, and jq is the query language. Neither needs your program.

Store the conversation. Rebuild the policy. ​

The session holds user, assistant and tool messages. It does not hold the system message.

Two reasons the system message stays out:

  1. It is policy for this run. If AGENTS.md changed since yesterday, the agent should follow the new rules, not replay the old ones.
  2. It must appear once. A program that both stores it and rebuilds it sends two on resume, and the second contradicts the first.

The rule generalises: store facts, rebuild decisions.

Resume is a slice, and the slice is where the bug is ​

The obvious implementation loads the history, appends it to the new request, and then records "everything" afterwards. That records the loaded history a second time:

  turn 1:  file = [u1, a1]
  resume:  history = [system, u1, a1, u2]
  save:    history[1:] = [u1, a1, u2]      ← u1 and a1 written again
  file =   [u1, a1, u1, a1, u2]

The next run sends u1, a1, u1, a1, u2, so the model sees the conversation twice, the context fills twice as fast, and nothing looks obviously wrong.

The fix is one number. Remember how many messages were loaded, and save only what comes after them:

go
prior := rec.Load()
history := append([]Message{{Role: RoleSystem, Content: system}}, prior...)
history = append(history, userMessage)
// ...
for _, m := range res.History[len(prior)+1:] {
	rec.Append(m)
}

len(prior)+1 skips the system message and the loaded history in one expression. That +1 is the chapter.

Tool pairs cross run boundaries too ​

A conversation with a tool call and no result is invalid: providers reject it. A resumed conversation is no different, which means the session must record assistant messages with their tool calls, not only the results.

{"role":"assistant","toolCalls":[{"id":"call_1","name":"read","arguments":"..."}]}
{"role":"tool","toolCallId":"call_1","content":"alpha"}

Record one and not the other, and the next run fails with a message about orphaned tool calls, three chapters after the bug was introduced.

Why a Recorder interface ​

The loop does not know where history lives. It is handed a history and returns a longer one. Sessions are a layer around the loop, which is why this chapter adds one file and edits main, and touches neither the loop nor the provider.

LayerKnows aboutDoes not know about
loopmessages, tools, providersfiles, paths, formats
sessiona file, append, loadthe loop, the model, tools
mainflags, wiringneither implementation detail

What this chapter does not do ​

  • No branching. One file is one linear conversation.
  • No compaction. The file grows forever; chapter 07 starts deleting from the request while keeping the file intact.
  • No concurrency. Two processes appending to one session interleave, and nothing here prevents it.

That last gap is worth naming rather than hiding. It is why pi locks its session files (proper-lockfile in its dependency list) and why this course defers it.

Where the real implementations go further ​

ConcernpiPiG
Session shapetree, every entry has a parentported tree
Branching and forkingcopy a subtree into a new fileported
Compactiona summary entry replaces older messages in the requestported
Lockingproper-lockfileported

The tree is what makes branching and compaction cheap. This chapter uses a line, which is the honest minimum and enough for eleven chapters.

Self-check ​

  1. Why does an append-only log beat a snapshot after a crash? (A session is a log, not a snapshot)
  2. Name the two reasons the system message is not stored. (Store the conversation. Rebuild the policy.)
  3. What exactly does len(prior)+1 skip? (Resume is a slice, and the slice is where the bug is)
  4. Which two records must both be written for a tool call, and what happens if one is missing? (Tool pairs cross run boundaries too)
  5. What does this chapter deliberately not handle? (What this chapter does not do)
